problem: Vanilla federated learning learns one global model, which degrades under non-IID data across robots in different terrains. Prior clustered FL methods infer data similarity indirectly from model weights or gradients and need multiple rounds or multiple models broadcast, so they are costly in bandwidth, and they are not tested on real robots.
motivation: Outdoor robots often have limited, intermittent upload bandwidth, so uploading raw data to a central server is impractical, and one global model may serve some environments poorly. Directly measuring similarity of the robots' visual data, rather than of their weights, could allow cheap and accurate grouping of robots.
key_idea: Each robot uploads its local model together with the mean ResNet-18 embedding of its images, and the server clusters robots with DBSCAN on these embeddings and averages models only within each cluster.
insight: Grouping robots by data-embedding similarity makes each cluster approximately IID, so plain averaging within a cluster avoids the negative transfer of FedAvg. In Table 1, FedAvg has higher loss than local training (WayFAST 0.007871 vs 0.006853), while Fed-EC reaches 0.004621, close to central at 0.004021, with an IPR of 100%. The mean embedding is a single vector, so clustering adds essentially no communication cost. Uploading model weights is much cheaper than uploading raw rosbags.
method: Mean embedding: each robot encodes its local images with a pretrained ResNet-18 and averages them into one vector that represents its data distribution
Local training: each robot trains its navigation model (WayFAST or BADGR) locally for 5 epochs per round and uploads the weights plus the mean embedding via WiFi

DBSCAN clustering: the server clusters robots by Euclidean distance between mean embeddings, with a manually tuned distance threshold and min points 2; the number of clusters is not preset, and noise points keep using their local model

Cluster aggregation: the server averages local weights within each cluster (FedAvg-style) and sends each robot its cluster model; embeddings are re-shared every round so cluster membership tracks changing environments
New-robot transfer: a new robot sends only its mean embedding, gets assigned to a cluster, and receives that cluster model without retraining
Navigation: the learned traversability (WayFAST) or collision (BADGR) predictions feed a nonlinear MPC with the kinodynamic model to reach a GPS goal

setting.backbone: WayFAST CNN and BADGR (trained from scratch, federated); ResNet-18 (pretrained, frozen) for embeddings; DBSCAN for clustering
setting.training_data: Real-world data collected by manual driving of one Terrasentia robot in semi-urban, forest-like and urban terrains, shuffled and split into 9 partitions (450-1000 samples each) to mimic 9 robots; later runs add data collected in previous runs
setting.observation: Front-facing ZED2 RGB + depth images (120° FOV), IMU, GNSS, wheel encoders
setting.action_space: MPC-generated continuous velocity commands toward a GPS goal

numbers_note: The paper reports only an in-house real-robot GPS-goal navigation task, given as successful runs out of 5 per environment (Table 3), plus validation loss and IPR. It does not use a canonical benchmark, so no benchmark entries are listed. Fed-EC WayFAST succeeded 5/5 in the forest and 3/5 in the parking lot; BADGR 4/5 and 3/5.
results: Fed-EC matches centralized learning on navigation (forest: WayFAST 5/5 vs central 5/5, BADGR 4/5 vs 4/5) and beats FedAvg (3/5 and 2/5) and local (2/5 and 2/5). Validation loss is lower than FedAvg and local for both models (WayFAST 0.004621 vs FedAvg 0.007871; BADGR 0.530927 vs FedAvg 1.877938). Uploading model weights takes 42 s for 78 MB versus 20 min 8 s for 1.8 GB of raw rosbag, the claimed 23x reduction.
limitations: Only one physical robot; the 'nine robots' are data partitions of it, and the tests are 5 trials per setting, so the statistics are weak
The DBSCAN distance threshold is manually tuned, and performance in the data-scarce parking lot is still lower than in the forest for all methods
BADGR loss is still well above central, and a 23x reduction compares raw data against weights, not against other clustered FL methods, which are not benchmarked
